Name: Nyasasaurus parringtoni
Author: Nesbitt et al.
Material: Vertebrae, fragmentary sacral ribs and incomplete humerus. Referred vertebrae (uncertain)
Reference: Nesbitt, Barrett, Werning, Sidor and Charig, (2013). The oldest dinosaur? A Middle Triassic dinosauriform from Tanzania.
Gen Info: Nyasasaurus parringtoni lived around 243 million years ago during the Middle Triassic and is considered one of the earliest known dinosaurs or very close relatives of true dinosaurs. It was discovered in present-day Tanzania. Although only fragmentary remains are known, its bone structure shows signs of rapid growth, a key dinosaur trait. It was a small, lightly built animal with long hind limbs, suggesting it moved on two legs and was capable of quick, agile movement. Nyasasaurus is extremely important because it helps scientists understand how and when dinosaurs first evolved from earlier archosaurs.
Habitat: Open floodplains and grassy areas near rivers.

Name: Alwalkeria maleriensis
Author: Chatterjee & Creisler
Material: Dorsal vertebra, incomplete femur, astragalus.
Reference: Chatterjee and Creisler, (1994). Alwalkeria (Theropoda) and Morturneria (Plesiosauria), new names for preoccupied Walkeria Chatterjee, 1987 and Turneria Chatterjee and Small, 1989.
Gen Info: Alwalkeria maleriensis lived during the Late Triassic about 230 million years ago in what is now India. It was a small, slender, bipedal dinosaur or close dinosaur relative with a long tail used for balance. Its teeth show a mix of shapes, indicating a flexible diet. Alwalkeria was likely an active and alert animal, able to move quickly to escape predators or search for food. It represents an early stage in dinosaur evolution, before strict specialization into carnivores or herbivores.

Name: Asylosaurus yalensis
Author: Galton
Material: Partial skeleton and humerus fragment, three fragmentary left ischia and phalanx.
Reference: Galton, Peter (2007). "Notes on the remains of archosaurian reptiles, mostly basal sauropodomorph dinosaurs, from the 1834 fissure fill (Rhaetian, Upper Triassic) at Clifton in Bristol, southwest England".
Gen Info: Asylosaurus yalensis lived during the Late Triassic in what is now the United Kingdom. It was a small, early ornithischian dinosaur, making it important for understanding the origins of plant-eating dinosaurs. Asylosaurus had a lightly built body and likely moved mainly on two legs, though it may have used all four limbs when feeding. Its jaw and teeth were adapted for processing plant material, suggesting a herbivorous lifestyle.

Name: Bagualosaurus agudoensis
Author: Pretto, Langer & Schultz
Material: Partial skeleton with skull fragments.
Reference: Flávio A. Pretto; Max C. Langer; Cesar L. Schultz (2018). "A new dinosaur (Saurischia: Sauropodomorpha) from the Late Triassic of Brazil provides insights on the evolution of sauropodomorph body plan".
Gen Info: Bagualosaurus agudoensis lived about 230 million years ago during the Late Triassic in present-day Brazil. It was an early sauropodomorph dinosaur and helps explain how small, bipedal dinosaurs evolved into massive long-necked giants. Bagualosaurus had a moderately long neck, strong limbs, and a robust body. It could likely walk on two legs but was beginning to adapt to a more four-legged posture.

Name: Blikanasaurus cromptoni
Author: Galton & van Heerden
Material: Epipodium and pes, referred right metatarsal and ilium (uncertain)
Reference: McPhee, B.W., Bordy, E.M., Sciscio, L., Choiniere, J.N. (2017). The sauropodomorph biostratigraphy of the Elliot Formation of southern Africa: Tracking the evolution of Sauropodomorpha across the Triassic–Jurassic boundary.
Gen Info: Blikanasaurus cromptoni lived near the end of the Triassic in southern Africa. It was one of the largest dinosaurs of its time and an early relative of later sauropods. This dinosaur had a very heavy, solid body and thick limb bones designed to support its weight. Unlike many early dinosaurs, Blikanasaurus likely moved mostly on four legs and grew rapidly, showing that large body size evolved very early in dinosaur history.

Name: Buriolestes schultzi
Author: Furtado Cabreira et al.
Material: Majority of skeleton with partial skull, referred almost complete skeleton with skull.
Reference: Müller, Langer, Bronzati, Pacheco, Cabreira & Dias-Da-Silva (2018). Early evolution of sauropodomorphs: anatomy and phylogenetic relationships of a remarkably well-preserved dinosaur from the Upper Triassic of southern Brazil.
Gen Info: Buriolestes schultzi lived about 230 million years ago during the Late Triassic in what is now southern Brazil. It is one of the earliest known sauropodomorph dinosaurs and is especially important because it shows that the first members of this group were not plant-eaters. Buriolestes was small, lightly built, and fully bipedal, with long hind legs and a slender tail that helped with balance. Its skull had sharp, curved teeth adapted for hunting, indicating an active and agile lifestyle. This dinosaur demonstrates that the lineage leading to giant herbivorous sauropods originally began as carnivorous animals.
Habitat: Open floodplains and lightly forested environments

Name: Camelotia borealis
Author: Galton
Material: Partial skeleton without skull.
Reference: P. M. Galton. (1985). Notes on the Melanorosauridae, a family of large prosauropod dinosaurs (Saurischia: Sauropodomorpha).
Gen Info: Camelotia borealis lived during the Late Triassic in present-day England. It was an early sauropodomorph dinosaur that shows the transition from small, fast-moving dinosaurs to larger-bodied herbivores. Camelotia had a long neck, a relatively heavy body, and strong limbs. It likely moved mainly on two legs but could use all four limbs when feeding. Its teeth were adapted for eating plants, suggesting a primarily herbivorous diet. Camelotia was slower and more robust than earlier dinosaur ancestors.

Name: Camposaurus arizonensis
Author: Hunt et al.
Material: Right and left distal ends of tibia and fibula fused with their respective astragalocalcanea.
Reference: Ezcurra, M.D.; Brusatte, S.L. (2011). "Taxonomic and phylogenetic reassessment of the early neotheropod dinosaur Camposaurus arizonensis from the Late Triassic of North America".
Gen Info: Camposaurus arizonensis was a small predatory dinosaur from the Late Triassic of what is now Arizona in the United States. It is one of the earliest known theropods in North America. Camposaurus had a slender body, long legs, and a lightweight skeleton, making it well suited for fast running. It walked exclusively on two legs and relied on speed and sharp teeth to catch prey. Despite its small size, it was likely an efficient hunter.
Habitat: Arid and semi-arid regions with sparse vegetation

Name: Chindesaurus bryansmalli
Author: Long & Murry
Material: Partial skeleton and several single bones.
Reference: Long and Murry, (1995). "Late Triassic (Carnian and Norian) tetrapods from the Southwestern United States."
Gen Info: Chindesaurus bryansmalli lived around 225 million years ago during the Late Triassic in the southwestern United States. It was a medium-sized early theropod or close relative of true theropods. Chindesaurus had long hind limbs, a strong tail for balance, and grasping hands with claws. Its body was built for agility, allowing it to pursue prey in open environments. It occupied the role of a mid-level predator in its ecosystem.
Habitat: River floodplains and open woodland areas

Name: Chromogisaurus novasi
Author: Ezcurra
Material: Partial skeleton (vertebrae, limb bones and other fragments).
Reference: Ezcurra, M. D. (2010). A new early dinosaur (Saurischia: Sauropodomorpha) from the Late Triassic of Argentina: a reassessment of dinosaur origin and phylogeny.
Gen Info: Chromogisaurus novasi lived during the Late Triassic in what is now Argentina. It was a small, early sauropodomorph closely related to the ancestors of later giant dinosaurs. Chromogisaurus had a lightly built body, a relatively long neck, and slender limbs. It was capable of bipedal movement and likely spent much of its time foraging. Its anatomy shows an early stage in the evolution toward larger, more specialized herbivorous dinosaurs.

Name: Coelophysis bauri
Author: Cope
Material: At least 1000 individuals (include complete skeletons).
Reference:
Cope, (1889). On a new genus of Triassic Dinosauria.
Mortimer - Theropod database (online).
Gen Info: Coelophysis bauri lived during the Late Triassic, around 215 million years ago, and is one of the best-known early theropod dinosaurs. Fossils have been found in large numbers in what is now the southwestern United States, suggesting it may have lived or hunted in groups. Coelophysis had a long, narrow skull filled with sharp teeth, a lightweight skeleton, and long hind limbs adapted for speed. It was an agile predator capable of catching small, fast-moving prey and is often considered a classic example of early carnivorous dinosaurs.

Name: Coloradisaurus brevis
Author: Lambert
Material: Two partial skeletons with skulls.
Reference: Apaldetti, C., Martinez, R. N., Pol, D., & Souter, T. (2014). Redescription of the Skull of Coloradisaurus brevis (Dinosauria, Sauropodomorpha) from the Late Triassic Los Colorados Formation of the Ischigualasto-Villa Union Basin, northwestern Argentina.
Gen Info: Coloradisaurus brevis lived during the Late Triassic in what is now Argentina. It was an early sauropodomorph dinosaur closely related to Plateosaurus. Coloradisaurus had a long neck, a relatively bulky body, and strong limbs. Although it could likely move on two legs, it probably spent much of its time walking on all fours while feeding. Its teeth were adapted for plant consumption, indicating a fully herbivorous lifestyle.

Name: Daemonosaurus chauliodus
Author: Sues et al.
Material: Skull, cervical vertebrae and cervical rib fragments.
Reference: Sues, H.-D., Nesbitt, S.J., Berman, D.S., Henrici, A.M. (2011). A late-surviving basal theropod dinosaur from the latest Triassic of North America.
Gen Info: Daemonosaurus chauliodus lived around 205 million years ago at the end of the Triassic in present-day New Mexico. It was a small but unusual theropod with a very short skull and large, forward-pointing teeth. These features suggest it had a specialized feeding strategy compared to other early predators. Daemonosaurus was lightly built and bipedal, and it likely preyed on small vertebrates in its environment.

Name: Efraasia minor
Author: Yates
Material: Large part of skeleton, referred several individuals.
Reference: Yates, A. M. (2003). The species taxonomy of the sauropodomorph dinosaurs from the Lowenstein Formation (Norian, Late Triassic) of Germany.
Gen Info: Efraasia minor lived during the Late Triassic in what is now Germany. It was an early sauropodomorph dinosaur that shows a mix of primitive and more advanced features. Efraasia had a long neck, a moderately heavy body, and strong hind limbs. It could walk both bipedally and quadrupedally depending on activity. This dinosaur played an important role as a medium-sized herbivore in its ecosystem.

Name: Eocursor parvus
Author: Butler, Smith & Norman
Material: Partial skeleton with skull fragments.
Reference: Butler, R.J., Smith, R.M.H., Norman, D.B. (2007). A primitive ornithischian dinosaur from the Late Triassic of South Africa, and the early evolution and diversification of Ornithischia.
Gen Info: Eocursor parvus lived during the Late Triassic in what is now South Africa. It was a small, early ornithischian dinosaur and one of the earliest members of this major dinosaur group. Eocursor had a lightly built body, long legs, and was well adapted for fast running. It likely relied on speed to avoid predators and fed on low-growing vegetation.
Habitat: Open grasslands and lightly wooded plains

Name: Eodromaeus murphi
Author: Martínez et al.
Material: Several individuals (large part of skeleton with skull).
Reference: Martinez, R. N., Sereno, P. C., Alcober, O. A., Colombi, C. E., Renne, P. R., Montanez, I. P., & Currie, B. S. (2011). A Basal Dinosaur from the Dawn of the Dinosaur Era in Southwestern Pangaea.
Gen Info: Eodromaeus murphi lived around 231 million years ago during the Late Triassic in what is now Argentina. It was a small, agile theropod dinosaur considered one of the earliest true dinosaurs. Eodromaeus had a lightweight body, long legs, and sharp teeth, making it an efficient predator. Its skeletal structure shows a mix of primitive and advanced features, giving scientists important insight into early dinosaur evolution.

Name: Eoraptor lunensis
Author: Sereno et al.
Material: Almost complete skeleton with skull, referred several individuals.
Reference: Sereno, P. C., Martínez, R. N., & Alcober, O. A. (2013). Osteology of Eoraptor lunensis (Dinosauria, Sauropodomorpha).
Gen Info: Eoraptor lunensis lived approximately 231 million years ago during the Late Triassic in present-day Argentina. It is one of the most primitive known dinosaurs and provides key information about the origins of both theropods and sauropodomorphs. Eoraptor was small, lightly built, and bipedal, with a long tail for balance and sharp, slightly serrated teeth suitable for a flexible diet.

Name: Eucnemesaurus entaxonis
Author: McPhee et al.
Material: Partial skeleton (vertebrae, right ilium, left ischium, right femur and fragments of the left and other fragments).
Reference: McPhee et al. (2015). A second species of Eucnemesaurus Van Hoepen, 1920 (Dinosauria, Sauropodomorpha): new information on the diversity and evolution of the sauropodomorph fauna of South Africa’s lower Elliot Formation (latest Triassic).
Gen Info: Eucnemesaurus entaxonis lived during the Late Triassic in what is now South Africa. It was a large, early sauropodomorph with robust limb bones and a relatively heavy body. Eucnemesaurus was likely primarily quadrupedal but could rear up on its hind legs when feeding. It was an important herbivore in its ecosystem, helping shape vegetation patterns.
Habitat: Open plains and lightly wooded areas

Name: Eucnemesaurus fortis
Author: van Hoepen
Material: At least three individuals (partial skeletons).
Reference: Yates, A. M. (2007). Solving a dinosaurian puzzle: the identity of Aliwalia rex Galton.
Gen Info: Eucnemesaurus fortis lived in the Late Triassic of South Africa. Similar to its close relative E. entaxonis, it was a large, sturdy sauropodomorph with strong limbs and a robust frame. It walked mainly on four legs and likely foraged for a variety of plant material. Its size made it relatively safe from smaller predators.

Name: Gnathovorax cabreirai
Author: Pacheco et al.
Material: Almost complete and partially articulated skeleton with skull.
Reference: Pacheco, Cristian; Müller, Rodrigo; Langer, Max; Pretto, Flávio; Kerber, Leonardo; da Silva, Sérgio Dias (2019). "Gnathovorax cabreirai: a new early dinosaur and the origin and initial radiation of predatory dinosaurs".
Gen Info: Gnathovorax cabreirai lived around 233 million years ago during the Late Triassic in what is now Brazil. It was a medium-sized early theropod with a long tail, slender limbs, and sharp teeth. Gnathovorax was built for speed and agility, likely hunting small vertebrates and invertebrates. Its discovery provides important insight into early predatory dinosaur evolution in Gondwana.

Name: Gojirasaurus quayi
Author: Carpenter
Material: Pubis and tibia.
Reference: Mortimer - Theropod database (online).
Gen Info: Gojirasaurus quayi lived during the Late Triassic, around 210 million years ago, in what is now New Mexico, USA. It was a large early theropod with a long, powerful tail, strong hind limbs, and a lightly built body adapted for running and hunting. Gojirasaurus had sharp teeth and claws, indicating a carnivorous diet. It represents one of the earliest large predatory dinosaurs in North America.

Name: Guaibasaurus candelariensis
Author: Bonaparte, Ferigolo & Ribeiro
Material: Three partial skeletons (without skull).
Reference: Langer, M. C., Bittencourt, J. S., & Schultz, C. L. (2010). A reassessment of the basal dinosaur Guaibasaurus candelariensis, from the Late Triassic Caturrita Formation of south Brazil.
Gen Info: Guaibasaurus candelariensis lived around 225 million years ago in what is now southern Brazil. This small to medium-sized early saurischian shows characteristics of both theropods and sauropodomorphs. Guaibasaurus had a slender body, long tail, and sharp teeth, indicating a primarily carnivorous lifestyle, though it may have occasionally eaten plants.

Name: Herrerasaurus ischigualastensis
Author: Reig
Material: At least several individuals (skeletons and skulls).
Reference: Mortimer - Theropod database (online).
Gen Info: Herrerasaurus ischigualastensis lived approximately 231 million years ago in the Late Triassic of Argentina. It is one of the earliest known true theropods and a top predator of its ecosystem. Herrerasaurus was medium-sized, bipedal, and built for speed, with a long tail for balance and sharp, serrated teeth. It was an agile hunter capable of taking down prey larger than itself.

Name: Ingentia prima
Author: Apaldetti et al.
Material: Two fragmentary skeletons.
Reference: Apaldetti, Cecilia; Martínez, Ricardo N.; Cerda, Ignatio A.; Pol, Diego; Alcober, Oscar (2018). "An early trend towards gigantism in Triassic sauropodomorph dinosaurs".
Gen Info: Ingentia prima lived about 210 million years ago during the Late Triassic in present-day Argentina. It was one of the earliest giant sauropodomorphs, with a long neck and massive body. Ingentia was quadrupedal and fed on high-growing vegetation, showing early adaptations for gigantism seen later in sauropods. Its discovery demonstrates that large size evolved earlier than previously thought.

Name: Isanosaurus attavipachi
Author: Buffetaut et al.
Material: Vertebrae, neural arch, chevron bones, fragmentary ribs, right sternal plate, right scapula and left femur.
Reference: Buffetaut, E., Suteethorn, V., Cuny, G., Tong, H., Le Loeuff, J., Khansubha, S., & Jongautchariyakul, S. (2000). The earliest known sauropod dinosaur.
Gen Info: Isanosaurus attavipachi was a primitive sauropod dinosaur that lived during the Late Triassic period, around 210 million years ago, in what is now Thailand. It is considered one of the earliest representatives of long-necked dinosaurs. It had a robust body, a long neck, and an extended tail that helped with balance. The dinosaur walked on four strong legs, well adapted to support its weight. Although it was smaller than later giant sauropods, it was large for its time and represents an important stage in the evolution of massive herbivorous dinosaurs.
Habitat: Plains and forested areas near rivers

Name: Jaklapallisaurus asymmetrica
Author: Novas et al.
Material: Vertebrae, distal right femur, right tibia, astragalus, right metatarsals I–IV and two pedal phalanges. Referred distal end of right femur.
Reference: Novas, F. E., Ezcurra, M. D., Chatterjee, S., & Kutty, T. S. (2011). New dinosaur species from the Upper Triassic Upper Maleri and Lower Dharmaram formations of Central India.
Gen Info: Jaklapallisaurus asymmetrica lived during the Late Triassic in what is now India. It was a small to medium-sized sauropodomorph with a long neck and slender limbs. Jaklapallisaurus was likely bipedal but could also walk on all fours while feeding. Its teeth were adapted for plant consumption, indicating a herbivorous diet. It represents an early stage in the evolution of large-bodied sauropodomorphs.

Name: Kholumolumo ellenbergerorum
Author: de Fabrègues & Allain
Material: At least several individuals.
Reference: Claire Peyre de Fabrègues & Ronan Allain (2020) Kholumolumo ellenbergerorum, gen. et sp. nov., a new early sauropodomorph from the lower Elliot Formation (Upper Triassic) of Maphutseng, Lesotho.
Gen Info: Kholumolumo ellenbergerorum lived around 200 million years ago in present-day Lesotho, southern Africa. It was a large early sauropodomorph with a long neck and massive body, walking primarily on four legs. Its heavy build suggests it could feed on taller vegetation, making it one of the first large herbivores of its ecosystem.
Habitat: Semi-arid plains and lightly forested areas

Name: Lepidus praecisio
Author: Nesbitt & Ezcurra
Material: Distal tibia, distal fibula, astragalocalcaneum, referred femoral fragment and partial maxilla.
Reference: Nesbitt, S.J., Ezcurra, M.D. (2015). The early fossil record of dinosaurs in North America: A new neotheropod from the base of the Upper Triassic Dockum Group of Texas.
Gen Info: Lepidus praecisio lived during the Late Triassic in what is now the southwestern United States. It was a small, agile theropod with a slender body, long tail, and sharp teeth adapted for hunting. Lepidus was bipedal and likely hunted small vertebrates and insects, playing the role of a mid-level predator in its environment.

Name: Lessemsaurus sauropoides
Author: Bonaparte
Material: Several fragmentary skeletons.
Reference: Apaldetti, C., Martínez, R. N., Cerda, I. A., Pol, D., & Alcober, O. (2018). An early trend towards gigantism in Triassic sauropodomorph dinosaurs.
Gen Info: Lessemsaurus sauropoides lived around 210 million years ago in what is now Argentina. It was an early sauropodomorph with a long neck, robust limbs, and a relatively large body. Lessemsaurus was quadrupedal and primarily herbivorous, feeding on ferns and other plants. It represents an early step in the evolution of giant sauropods.

Name: Leyesaurus marayensis
Author: Apaldetti et al.
Material: Almost complete skull and fragmentary skeleton.
Reference: Apaldetti, C., Martínez, R.N., Alcober, O.A., Pol, D. (2011). A New Basal Sauropodomorph (Dinosauria: Saurischia) from Quebrada del Barro Formation (Marayes-El Carrizal Basin), Northwestern Argentina.
Gen Info: Leyesaurus marayensis lived during the Late Triassic in present-day Argentina. It was a small to medium-sized sauropodomorph with a long neck and lightly built body. Leyesaurus could move bipedally or quadrupedally while feeding. Its teeth were adapted for herbivory, allowing it to graze on low vegetation.

Name: Liliensternus liliensterni
Author: Welles
Material: Two incomplete skeletons and incomplete skull.
Reference: Mortimer - Theropod database (online).
Gen Info: Liliensternus liliensterni lived during the Late Triassic in what is now Germany. It was a medium-sized theropod with a slender, agile body, long legs, and sharp teeth. Liliensternus was bipedal and likely hunted small to medium-sized animals, including early reptiles and possibly other small dinosaurs. Its anatomy shows early adaptations for speed and predatory efficiency.

Name: Lucianovenator bonoi
Author: Martínez & Apaldetti
Material: Fragmentary skeleton, referred 3 fragmentary skeletons and proximal tibia (uncertain)
Reference: Martínez, R. N., & Apaldetti, C. (2017). A Late Norian—Rhaetian Coelophysid Neotheropod (Dinosauria, Saurischia) from the Quebrada Del Barro Formation, Northwestern Argentina.
Gen Info: Lucianovenator bonoi lived around 230 million years ago in present-day Argentina. It was a small, agile early theropod with a lightweight body and long limbs built for running. Lucianovenator had sharp teeth for capturing prey and likely occupied the role of a mid-level predator in its ecosystem.
Habitat: River valleys and lightly forested plains

Name: Macrocollum itaquii
Author: Müller et al.
Material: Two almost complete skeletons with skulls and partial skeleton without skull.
Reference: Müller, R.T., Langer, M.C., Dias-da-Silva, S. (2018). "An exceptionally preserved association of complete dinosaur skeletons reveals the oldest long-necked sauropodomorphs".
Gen Info: Macrocollum itaquii lived during the Late Triassic in southern Brazil. It was a small, early sauropodomorph with an elongated neck and slender limbs, capable of bipedal movement but likely feeding on all fours. Its teeth were adapted for plant consumption, indicating herbivory. Macrocollum is one of the earliest known sauropodomorphs with a relatively long neck.

Name: Melanorosaurus readi
Author: Haughton
Material: Several fragmentary skeletons.
Reference: Galton PM, Van Heerden J, Yates AM (2005). "Postcranial Anatomy of Referred Specimens of Melanorosaurus".
Gen Info: Melanorosaurus readi lived during the Late Triassic in what is now South Africa. It was a large sauropodomorph with a long neck and massive body, walking primarily on four legs. Its robust limbs supported its heavy weight while feeding on tall vegetation. Melanorosaurus represents an early stage in the evolution toward giant Jurassic sauropods.

Name: Meroktenos thabanensis
Author: de Fabrègues & Allain
Material: Fragmentary skeleton, referred cervical vertebra, left ulna and radius (uncertain)
Reference: Peyre de Fabregues, C., Allain, R. (2016). New material and revision of Melanorosaurus thabanensis, a basal sauropodomorph from the Upper Triassic of Lesotho.
Gen Info: Meroktenos thabanensis lived around 210 million years ago in Lesotho, southern Africa. It was a medium to large-sized early sauropodomorph with a strong, heavy body and relatively long neck. Meroktenos likely fed on a variety of plants and walked quadrupedally, showing early adaptations toward gigantism.

Name: Mussaurus patagonicus
Author: Bonaparte & Vince
Material: At least more than 20 individuals (hatchlings to adults).
Reference: Otero, A., & Pol, D. (2013). Postcranial anatomy and phylogenetic relationships of Mussaurus patagonicus (Dinosauria, Sauropodomorpha).
Gen Info: Mussaurus patagonicus lived during the Late Triassic in what is now Argentina. It was a small to medium-sized sauropodomorph as an adult, though juveniles were tiny and likely lived in groups for protection. Mussaurus had a long neck and tail, walked both bipedally and quadrupedally, and fed on low-growing vegetation. It is notable for showing evidence of social behavior in early sauropodomorphs.

Name: Nambalia roychowdhurii
Author: Novas et al.
Material: At least three individuals.
Reference: Novas, F. E., Ezcurra, M. D., Chatterjee, S., & Kutty, T. S. (2010). New dinosaur species from the Upper Triassic Upper Maleri and Lower Dharmaram formations of Central India.
Gen Info: Nambalia roychowdhurii lived around 210 million years ago during the Late Triassic in present-day India. It was a small sauropodomorph with a long neck and slender limbs. Nambalia could move on two or four legs while feeding and had teeth adapted for plant consumption.

Name: Nhandumirim waldsangae
Author: Marsola et al.
Material: 3 dorsal vertebrae, 2 sacral vertebrae, 7 caudal vertebrae, chevron, pelvic and hind limb bones.
Reference: Marsola, J.C.A., Bittencourt, J.S.J., Butler, R., Da Rosa, A.A.S., Sayão, J.M., Langer, M.C. (2019). "A new dinosaur with theropod affinities from the Late Triassic Santa Maria Formation, South Brazil".
Gen Info: Nhandumirim waldsangae lived during the Late Triassic in what is now Brazil. It was a small, early sauropodomorph with a long neck and lightweight body. Nhandumirim was likely bipedal but may have occasionally used all fours to reach vegetation. Its discovery helps clarify early diversity in sauropodomorph evolution.

Name: Notatesseraeraptor frickensis
Author: Zahner & Brinkmann
Material: Partial skeleton and incomplete skull, referred teeth (uncertain), fragmentary skeleton with skull (uncertain)
Reference: Zahner, M., & Brinkmann, W. (2019). A Triassic averostran-line theropod from Switzerland and the early evolution of dinosaurs.
Gen Info: Notatesseraeraptor frickensis lived about 210 million years ago in what is now Switzerland. It was a small to medium-sized theropod with a slender body, long legs, and sharp teeth, adapted for speed and predation. Notatesseraeraptor is important for understanding early diversification of theropods in Europe.
Habitat: Semi-arid floodplains and lightly wooded areas

Name: Pampadromaeus barberenai
Author: Cabreira et al.
Material: Partial skeleton with incomplete skull. Referred femur.
Reference: Langer, Cabreira, Bittencourt and Schultz, (2011). A new eusaurischian from the Santa Maria Formation, Late Triassic of Brazil, highlights mosaic pattern of character evolution during the rise of dinosaurs. Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.
Gen Info: Pampadromaeus barberenai lived during the Late Triassic in present-day Brazil. It was a small, early sauropodomorph with a long neck, lightly built body, and herbivorous teeth. Pampadromaeus could likely move bipedally or quadrupedally while feeding and represents one of the earliest members of its group in South America.

Name: Panphagia protos
Author: Martinez & Alcober
Material: Partial skeleton with skull fragments (juvenile).
Reference: Martinez and Alcober, (2009). A basal sauropodomorph (Dinosauria: Saurischia) from the Ischigualasto Formation (Triassic, Carnian) and the early evolution of Sauropodomorpha.
Gen Info: Panphagia protos lived around 231 million years ago during the Late Triassic in what is now Argentina. It was a small, early sauropodomorph with a lightly built body, long tail, and slender limbs. Panphagia had both primitive and advanced traits and is considered one of the earliest known sauropodomorphs. Its teeth suggest it may have had an omnivorous diet.
Habitat: Open floodplains and lightly forested areas

Name: Pantydraco caducus
Author: Galton, Yates & Kermack
Material: Several partial skeletons.
Reference: Galton, P.M., Yates, A.M., and Kermack, D. (2007). "Pantydraco n. gen. for Thecodontosaurus caducus YATES, 2003, a basal sauropodomorph dinosaur from the Upper Triassic or Lower Jurassic of South Wales, UK.".
Gen Info: Pantydraco caducus lived during the Late Triassic in what is now Wales. It was a small, early sauropodomorph with a long neck and slender body. Pantydraco likely walked bipedally but may have fed using all fours. Its teeth were adapted for consuming plants, showing early herbivorous traits.

Name: Plateosauravus cullingworthi

Gen Info: Kaijiangosaurus lini was a large carnivorous theropod from the Middle Jurassic of China. It had a long, narrow skull with sharp, curved teeth and powerful forelimbs. Its overall body was built for active predation, capable of pursuing mid-sized herbivores. Fossil evidence suggests it occupied a top predator niche in forested and open plain ecosystems.

Name: Kileskus aristotocus
Author: Averianov et al.
Material: Skull fragments, few limb bones, referred vertebrae, chevron and fibula.
Reference: Averianov, A.O., Osochnikova, A., Skutschas, P., Krasnolutskii, S., Schellhorn, R., Schultz, J.A. & Martin, T. (2019). "New data on the tyrannosauroid dinosaur Kileskus from the Middle Jurassic of Siberia, Russia.".
Gen Info: Kileskus aristotocus was a small, basal tyrannosauroid theropod from the Middle Jurassic, lightly built with long limbs and a slender skull. It is considered an early relative of later tyrannosaurs, likely feeding on small vertebrates, insects, and possibly carrion. Agile and fast, it may have hunted in small groups or alone in forested habitats.

Name: Kulindadromeus zabaikalicus
Author: Godefroit et al.
Material: At least six skulls and hundreds of disarticulated skeletons.
Reference: Godefroit et al. (2014). A Jurassic ornithischian dinosaur from Siberia with both feathers and scales.
Gen Info: Kulindadromeus zabaikalicus was a small feathered ornithischian from Siberia, with a combination of scales and filamentous feathers covering its body. Bipedal and agile, it had specialized leaf-shaped teeth for browsing plants, and its feathers suggest possible thermoregulation or display functions.

Name: Lapparentosaurus madagascariensis
Author: Bonaparte
Material: At least five individuals (juvenile).
Reference: MANNION, P. D. (2010). A revision of the sauropod dinosaur genus “Bothriospondylus” with a redescription of the type material of the Middle Jurassic form “B. madagascariensis.
Gen Info: Lapparentosaurus madagascariensis was a large sauropod from Madagascar, characterized by its extremely long neck, massive limbs, and elongated tail. It likely fed on high vegetation, such as conifers and cycads, and moved in small herds to provide protection from predators. Its robust skeleton suggests it could support a huge body while foraging on floodplains.

Name: Leshansaurus qianweiensis
Author: Li, Peng, Ye, Jiang & Huang
Material: Partial skeleton with incomplete skull. Referred femur (juvenile).
Reference: Li, Peng, Ye, Jiang and Huang, (2009). A new carnosaur from the Late Jurassic of Qianwei, Sichuan, China.
Gen Info: Leshansaurus qianweiensis was a large, carnivorous theropod from the Middle Jurassic of China. With a robust skull, large serrated teeth, and strong legs, it was likely a top predator preying on medium- to large-sized herbivorous dinosaurs. Its presence suggests a complex predator-prey ecosystem with forested and open habitats.

Name: Loricatosaurus priscus
Author: Maidment et al.
Material: Two partial skeletons.
Reference: Maidment, S.C.R., Norman, D.B., Barrett, P.M., & Upchurch, P. (2008) "Systematics and phylogeny of Stegosauria (Dinosauria: Ornithischia)".
Gen Info: Loricatosaurus priscus was a medium to large stegosaur from the Late Jurassic of Europe, with strong dorsal plates and spiked tail for defense. It had a moderately long neck and sturdy limbs for supporting its body while browsing on ferns, cycads, and low shrubs. Its armor helped protect it from theropod predators.

Name: Magnosaurus nethercombensis
Author: von Huene
Material: Partial skeleton (dentaries, impressions of ribs, hind limb bones and other fragments).
Reference: Benson, R. B. J. (2010). The osteology of Magnosaurus nethercombensis (Dinosauria, Theropoda) from the Bajocian (Middle Jurassic) of the United Kingdom and a re-examination of the oldest records of tetanurans.
Gen Info: Magnosaurus nethercombensis was a medium-sized theropod from the Middle Jurassic of Europe. It had long, slender limbs, a lightly built body, and sharp serrated teeth. It likely hunted small to medium herbivorous dinosaurs and possibly scavenged larger carcasses.

Name: Manidens condorensis
Author: Pol, Rauhut & Becerra
Material: Partial disarticulated skull and skeleton. Referred isolated teeth.
Reference: Sereno, P. (2012). "Taxonomy, morphology, masticatory function and phylogeny of heterodontosaurid dinosaurs".
Gen Info: Manidens condorensis was a small basal ornithischian from the Late Jurassic of Argentina. It was bipedal with a small skull, specialized teeth for grinding plants, and agile limbs for escaping predators. Likely lived in small groups and fed on low-growing vegetation such as ferns and cycads.

Name: Megalosaurus bucklandii
Author: Mantell
Formations: Taynton Limestone, Chipping Norton Limestone, Sharp's Hill, Great Oolite Group
Material: Many individuals.

BENSON, R. B. J. (2010). A description of Megalosaurus bucklandii (Dinosauria: Theropoda) from the Bathonian of the UK and the relationships of Middle Jurassic theropods.

Gen Info: Megalosaurus bucklandii was a large, early-described theropod from the Middle Jurassic of England. It had a robust skull, serrated teeth, strong hind limbs, and likely preyed on medium to large herbivorous dinosaurs. Its fossils indicate it was one of the apex predators of its time.

Name: Alcovasaurus longispinus
Author: Galton & Carpenter
Material: Forty two vertebrae, sacrum, three anterior caudal centra, parts of both ilia and ischia, left pubis, right femur and dermal caudal spines. Referred large spike (uncertain)
Reference: Francisco Costa & OctÃvio Mateus (2019) Dacentrurine stegosaurs (Dinosauria): A new specimen of Miragaia longicollum from the Late Jurassic of Portugal resolves taxonomical validity and shows the occurrence of the clade in North America.
Gen Info: Alcovasaurus longispinus was a stegosaur with unusually long shoulder spines and a moderately armored back. Its body was built for slow movement while browsing on ferns and cycads, and the elongated spines may have been used for defense or display.

Name: Allosaurus europaeus
Author: Mateus et al.
Material: Posterior skull, sclerotic ring, posterior mandible, fourth to sixth cervical vertebrae, fourth to sixth cervical ribs.

Gen Info: Allosaurus europaeus was a large theropod from the Late Jurassic of Europe. Similar to North American Allosaurus, it had powerful jaws, serrated teeth, strong forelimbs, and was likely an apex predator feeding on large sauropods and ornithischians.

Name: Allosaurus fragilis
Author: Marsh

Madsen, J.H.Jr. (1993) [1976]. Allosaurus fragilis: A Revised Osteology.

Glut, Donald F. (1997). "Allosaurus". Dinosaurs: The Encyclopedia.
Gen Info: Allosaurus fragilis was one of the most famous Jurassic predators, with a large skull, sharp serrated teeth, strong arms, and muscular hind limbs. It could hunt large herbivorous dinosaurs either alone or possibly in packs, and occupied diverse habitats from plains to forests.

Name: Allosaurus jimmadseni
Author: Chure & Loewen
Material: At least several individuals (include almost complete skeletons and skulls).

Chure, (2000). A new species of Allosaurus from the Morrison Formation of Dinosaur National Monument (Utah-Colorado) and a revision of the theropod family Allosauridae.

Likely one of the top predators of its ecosystem, it could hunt large herbivorous dinosaurs and may have scavenged as well. Evidence suggests it could have lived and hunted in small groups, using intelligence and speed to tackle prey.

Name: Amanzia greppini
Author: Schwarz et al.
Material: At least four individuals.
Reference: Schwarz et al. (2020). Re-description of the sauropod dinosaur Amanzia (“Ornithopsis/Cetiosauriscus”) greppini n. gen. and other vertebrate remains from the Kimmeridgian (Late Jurassic) Reuchenette Formation of Moutier, Switzerland.
Gen Info: Amanzia greppini was a mid-sized sauropod with a long neck and massive body, living during the Late Jurassic in Europe. Its limbs were strong and columnar, supporting its heavy weight, and it likely browsed on conifers and other high vegetation. Its size offered protection from most predators, although juveniles were probably vulnerable.

Name: Anchiornis huxleyi
Author: Xu X. et al.
Material: At least more than 200 specimens.
Reference: Xu, X; Zhao, Q.; Norell, M.; Sullivan, C.; Hone, D.; Erickson, G.; Wang, X.; Han, F. & Guo, Y. (2009). "A new feathered maniraptoran dinosaur fossil that fills a morphological gap in avian origin".
Gen Info: Anchiornis huxleyi was a tiny feathered theropod from the Late Jurassic of China. It had wings on both its arms and legs, a feathered tail, and a small, delicate skull. Likely used feathers for display, thermoregulation, or primitive gliding. It preyed on insects and small vertebrates and may have lived in dense forests.

Name: Aorun zhaoi
Author: Choiniere et al.
Material: Partial skeleton with skull.
Reference: Choiniere, Clark, Forster, Norell, Eberth, Erickson, Chu & Xu. (2014). A juvenile specimen of a new coelurosaur (Dinosauria: Theropoda) from the Middle–Late Jurassic Shishugou Formation of Xinjiang, People’s Republic of China.
Gen Info: Aorun zhaoi was a small, fast-running theropod from the Late Jurassic of China. It had a lightly built body, long hind limbs, and sharp teeth for catching small vertebrates. Its agility and speed made it an effective predator of lizards, early mammals, and small dinosaurs.

Name: Apatosaurus ajax
Author: Marsh
Material: At least one partial skeleton with fragmentary skull. Referred other specimens (uncertain)
Reference: Tschopp, E., Mateus, O. & Benson, R.B.J. (2015) "A specimen-level phylogenetic analysis and taxonomic revision of Diplodocidae (Dinosauria, Sauropoda)".
Gen Info: Apatosaurus ajax was a giant sauropod with an extremely long neck and tail, heavy body, and column-like limbs. It fed on tall trees and shrubs, using its neck to reach high vegetation, and possibly for intraspecific display or combat. It moved slowly but could cover long distances in search of food.
Habitat: Floodplains, river valleys, lightly forested areas

Name: Apatosaurus louisae
Author: Holland
Material: At least four specimens (one almost complete skeleton).
Reference: Tschopp, E., Mateus, O. & Benson, R.B.J. (2015) "A specimen-level phylogenetic analysis and taxonomic revision of Diplodocidae (Dinosauria, Sauropoda)".
Gen Info: Apatosaurus louisae was one of the largest sauropods of the Late Jurassic. With a long neck, massive tail, and enormous body, it browsed on high vegetation, likely feeding on conifers, ferns, and cycads. Its robust body suggests it lived in herds for protection against predators like Allosaurus.

Name: Brachiosaurus altithorax
Author: Riggs
Material: Partial skeleton, referred other specimens also skull material.

Taylor, M.P. (2009) "A re-evaluation of Brachiosaurus altithorax Riggs 1903 (Dinosauria, Sauropoda) and its generic separation from Giraffatitan brancai (Janensch 1914)" .

Gen Info: Brachiosaurus altithorax was a colossal sauropod with extremely long forelimbs, giving it a giraffe-like posture. Its long neck allowed it to reach tall trees, feeding on high vegetation inaccessible to other herbivores. Fossils indicate it had a large body cavity for processing huge amounts of plant material.

Name: Brachytrachelopan mesai
Author: Rauhut et al.
Material: Partial skeleton (vertebrae, ribs, right ilium, and other fragments).

Gen Info: Brachytrachelopan mesai was a relatively short-necked sauropod, unlike most sauropods. Its neck was adapted for low browsing, feeding on ferns and shrubs. It had strong, compact limbs and likely lived in small herds or family groups to avoid predation.

Name: Brontosaurus excelsus
Author: Marsh
Material: Majority of skeleton, referred partial skeleton.
Reference: Tschopp, E., Mateus, O. & Benson, R.B.J. (2015) "A specimen-level phylogenetic analysis and taxonomic revision of Diplodocidae (Dinosauria, Sauropoda)".
Gen Info: Brontosaurus excelsus was a massive long-necked sauropod with a whip-like tail and pillar-like limbs. It could browse a wide range of vegetation, from low shrubs to tall trees. Fossil evidence suggests it may have moved in herds and communicated using low-frequency sounds to coordinate group movement.

Name: Brontosaurus parvus
Author: Tschopp, Mateus & Benson
Material: Two partial skeletons and probably one almost complete skeleton.
Reference: Tschopp, E., Mateus, O. & Benson, R.B.J. (2015) "A specimen-level phylogenetic analysis and taxonomic revision of Diplodocidae (Dinosauria, Sauropoda)".
Gen Info: Brontosaurus parvus was a medium-sized species of Brontosaurus with a similar body plan to other members of the genus. It had a long neck and tail for feeding and defense, and its body was robust, suggesting slow but steady movement across plains in search of food.

Name: Brontosaurus yahnahpin
Author: Tschopp, Mateus & Benson
Material: Partial skeleton.
Reference: Tschopp, E., Mateus, O. & Benson, R.B.J. (2015) "A specimen-level phylogenetic analysis and taxonomic revision of Diplodocidae (Dinosauria, Sauropoda)".
Gen Info: Brontosaurus yahnahpin was a Late Jurassic sauropod adapted for high browsing. Its long neck allowed it to reach tree canopies, while its massive tail could be used as a defensive weapon. Likely traveled in herds, providing safety in numbers.

Name: Caihong juji
Author: Hu et al.

Gen Info: Caihong juji was a small, feathered theropod from the Late Jurassic of China. Its feathers were iridescent, likely used for display or mating rituals. It had a small skull with sharp teeth and long legs for running. It likely preyed on insects and small vertebrates, possibly supplementing its diet with plant matter.

Name: Camarasaurus grandis
Author: Marsh

Gen Info: Camarasaurus grandis was a large, robust sauropod with a strong skull, broad teeth, and massive body. It fed on tough vegetation, such as cycads and conifers, and likely moved in herds. Its neck was moderately long, allowing it to browse a wide range of heights, and its skeletal structure supported heavy loads.

Name: Camarasaurus lentus
Author: Marsh
Material: At least several individuals also with skulls (include almost complete juvenile skeleton).
Reference: Ikejiri, T. (2005) "Distribution and biochronology of Camarasaurus (dinosauria, sauropoda) from the jurassic morrison Formation of the rocky mountain region".
Gen Info: Camarasaurus lentus was a medium to large sauropod, one of the most common herbivores of the Late Jurassic. With a robust build and spoon-shaped teeth, it could process large amounts of vegetation. Fossil evidence suggests it may have lived in herds to protect against predators like Allosaurus.
Habitat: River valleys, floodplains, lightly forested areas

Name: Camarasaurus supremus
Author: Cope
Material: Several individuals.
Reference: Ikejiri, T. (2005) "Distribution and biochronology of Camarasaurus (dinosauria, sauropoda) from the jurassic morrison Formation of the rocky mountain region".
Gen Info: Camarasaurus supremus was one of the largest species of Camarasaurus, a massive Late Jurassic sauropod. It had a long neck, strong limbs, and a large, box-shaped skull with robust teeth adapted for stripping leaves and branches. Its enormous body likely made it safe from most predators, though juveniles may have been vulnerable. It probably traveled in herds to forage and provide protection.

Name: Camptosaurus dispar
Author: Marsh
Material: Many individuals (include skulls and almost complete skeleton).
Reference: MCDONALD, A. T. (2011). The taxonomy of species assigned to Camptosaurus (Dinosauria: Ornithopoda).
Gen Info: Camptosaurus dispar was a common Late Jurassic ornithopod with the ability to walk bipedally or quadrupedally. It had a small head, leaf-shaped teeth, and strong limbs for running or supporting its body while browsing. Fossil evidence suggests it fed on low to mid-height vegetation and may have lived in social groups.

Name: Camptosaurus prestwichii
Author: Lydekker
Material: Partial skull and postcranium.
Reference: Carpenter, K., & Lamanna, M. C. (2015). The Braincase Assigned to the Ornithopod Dinosaur Uteodon McDonald, 2011, Reassigned to Dryosaurus Marsh, 1894: Implications for Iguanodontian Morphology and Taxonomy.
Gen Info: Camptosaurus prestwichii was a lightly built ornithopod with a small skull and teeth adapted for shredding plants. Agile and fast, it could escape predators while foraging in diverse environments. Its limbs allowed both bipedal running and quadrupedal browsing.

Name: Cathetosaurus lewisi
Author: Jensen
Material: A large part of skeleton.
Reference: Mateus, O., & Tschopp E. (2013). Cathetosaurus as a valid sauropod genus and comparisons with Camarasaurus.
Gen Info: Cathetosaurus lewisi was a sauropod related to Diplodocus, with a long neck and tail, robust limbs, and a relatively light skull. It could feed at multiple heights, browsing on ferns, cycads, and conifers. Likely lived in small herds to protect juveniles from predators.

Name: Ceratosaurus dentisulcatus
Author: Madsen & Welles
Material: A large part of skeleton with incomplete skull.
Reference: Madsen, J.H.; Welles, S.P. (2000). Ceratosaurus (Dinosauria, Theropoda): A Revised Osteology.
Gen Info: Ceratosaurus dentisulcatus was a medium to large theropod with a prominent nasal horn, blade-like teeth, and muscular hind limbs. It was a versatile predator, hunting medium-sized dinosaurs and possibly scavenging larger carcasses. Its sharp claws and powerful bite made it a formidable hunter.

Name: Ceratosaurus magnicornis
Author: Madsen & Welles
Material: Majority of skeleton with incomplete skull.
Reference: Madsen, J.H.; Welles, S.P. (2000). Ceratosaurus (Dinosauria, Theropoda): A Revised Osteology.
Gen Info: Ceratosaurus magnicornis was a large theropod with distinctive cranial ornamentation, serrated teeth, and strong legs for pursuit. Likely an apex predator in its ecosystem, it hunted large herbivorous dinosaurs and may have engaged in opportunistic scavenging.

Name: Ceratosaurus nasicornis
Author: Marsh
Material: Almost complete skull and partial skeleton, referred several (uncertain) other individuals.
Reference: Carrano, M. T., & Sampson, S. D. (2008). The Phylogeny of Ceratosauria (Dinosauria: Theropoda).
Gen Info: Ceratosaurus nasicornis was a medium-sized carnivorous theropod with a single nasal horn, robust jaws, and muscular limbs. It hunted mid-sized dinosaurs and small vertebrates, and its speed and agility made it an effective ambush predator.

Name: Chilesaurus diegosuarezi
Author: Novas et al.
Material: Several (or at least 13 (uncertain)) partial skeletons (also with skull fragments).
Reference: Novas, F.E., Salgado, L., Suárez, M., Agnolín, F.L., Ezcurra, M.D., Chimento, N.R., de la Cruz, R., Isasi, M.P., Vargas, A.O., Rubilar-Rogers, D. (2015). An enigmatic plant-eating theropod from the Late Jurassic period of Chile.
Gen Info: Chilesaurus diegosuarezi was a highly unusual herbivorous theropod from the Late Jurassic of Chile. It combined traits of theropods and ornithischians, had a beak-like snout, leaf-shaped teeth, and bipedal posture. Likely fed on ferns, cycads, and other low plants, living in semi-open habitats.

Name: Chungkingosaurus jiangbeiensis
Author: Dong, Zhou & Zhang
Material: Incomplete skeleton with skull fragments. Referred other individuals (uncertain)
Reference: MAIDMENT, S. C. R., & WEI, G. (2006). A review of the Late Jurassic stegosaurs (Dinosauria, Stegosauria) from the People’s Republic of China.
Gen Info: Chungkingosaurus jiangbeiensis was a small stegosaur with rows of plates and tail spikes. Its short neck and small head indicate it fed on low vegetation. Defensive tail spikes helped protect it from predators, while its medium body size allowed it to navigate forested areas.

Name: Coelurus fragilis
Author: Marsh
Material: Several fragmentary skeletons.
Reference: Carpenter, Miles, Ostrom and Cloward, (2005). Redescription of the small maniraptoran theropods Ornitholestes and Coelurus from the Upper Jurassic Morrison Formation of Wyoming.
Gen Info: Coelurus fragilis was a small, lightly built theropod with long limbs, a long tail for balance, and a small skull with sharp teeth. Agile and fast, it likely hunted small vertebrates and insects in open forests or plains.

Name: Compsognathus longipes

Peyer, (2003). A complete redescription of the French Compsognathus with special consideration of the anatomy of the hand.

Name: Daanosaurus zhangi
Author: Ye, Gao & Jiang

Gen Info: Daanosaurus zhangi was a small sauropod from the Early Jurassic of China. With a long neck, slender body, and column-like limbs, it browsed low to mid-height vegetation. Likely lived in small herds for protection, feeding on ferns, cycads, and conifers.

Name: Diplodocus carnegii
Author: Hatcher
Material: At least two skeletons.
Reference: Tschopp, E., Mateus, O. & Benson, R.B.J. (2015) "A specimen-level phylogenetic analysis and taxonomic revision of Diplodocidae (Dinosauria, Sauropoda).
Gen Info: Diplodocus carnegii was one of the longest sauropods, with an extremely long neck and tail, a small head, and a light, elongated body. It likely fed on high tree foliage, using its long neck to reach inaccessible plants. Its whip-like tail may have been used for defense or communication within herds.

Name: Diplodocus hallorum
Author: Tschopp, Mateus & Benson
Material: Partial skeleton, referred three partial skeletons.
Reference: Tschopp, E., Mateus, O. & Benson, R.B.J. (2015) "A specimen-level phylogenetic analysis and taxonomic revision of Diplodocidae (Dinosauria, Sauropoda).
Gen Info: Diplodocus hallorum (formerly Seismosaurus) was an enormous sauropod, one of the longest dinosaurs known. Its long neck and tail allowed it to feed over a wide area without moving its massive body. Likely traveled in herds and grazed on ferns, conifers, and other high vegetation.
Habitat: Floodplains, lightly forested areas, river valleys

Name: Draconyx loureiroi
Author: Mateus & Telles Antunes
Material: Fragmentary skeleton (teeth, caudal vertebrae, limb bones and fragments) referred two femora.
Reference: Mateus, O., & Telles Antunes, M. (2001). Draconyx loureiroi, a new camptosauridae (Dinosauria, Ornithopoda) from the Late Jurassic of Lourinhã, Portugal.
Gen Info: Draconyx loureiroi was a small to medium-sized ornithopod from the Late Jurassic of Portugal. It had strong hind limbs for running and a lightly built body for agility. Its leaf-shaped teeth and beak were adapted to strip low-growing vegetation, such as ferns and cycads. Likely a social animal, it may have lived in small herds to avoid predation.

Name: Dracopelta zbyszewskii
Author: Galton

Reference: Galton, P. M. (1980). Partial skeleton of Dracopelta zbyszewskii N. Gen. And N. SP., an ankylosaurian dinosaur from the Upper Jurassic of Portugal.
Gen Info: Dracopelta zbyszewskii was an early armored dinosaur with bony plates covering its back for defense. Small and stocky, it had a low-slung body and sturdy limbs, suggesting slow movement. Its armor provided protection against medium-sized predators, while it foraged for low-lying vegetation.

Name: Dryosaurus altus
Author: Marsh
Material: At least several skeletons and skulls.
Reference: Carpenter, K., Galton, P.M, (2018). "A photo documentation of bipedal ornithischian dinosaurs from the Upper Jurassic Morrison Formation, USA".
Gen Info: Dryosaurus altus was a medium-sized ornithopod from the Late Jurassic of North America. Lightly built with long legs and a slender tail, it could run quickly to escape predators. Its leaf-shaped teeth indicate it fed on ferns, cycads, and other low plants. Fossil evidence suggests it lived in groups for protection.
Habitat: Open plains, forest edges, lightly wooded areas

Name: Dryosaurus elderae
Author: Carpenter & Galton
Material: Partial skeleton with skull, partial juvenile skeleton with skull, braincase, left ilium, right scapula.
Reference: Carpenter, K., Galton, P.M, (2018). "A photo documentation of bipedal ornithischian dinosaurs from the Upper Jurassic Morrison Formation, USA".
Gen Info: Dryosaurus elderae was closely related to D. altus, small and agile, with specialized teeth for herbivory. Its strong hind limbs allowed it to sprint when threatened, and its moderately long tail helped with balance during bipedal locomotion. Likely foraged on low-growing plants.

Name: Giraffatitan brancai
Author: Paul
Material: Probably more than 30 individuals.
Reference: Taylor, M.P. (2009) "A re-evaluation of Brachiosaurus altithorax Riggs 1903 (Dinosauria, Sauropoda) and its generic separation from Giraffatitan brancai (Janensch 1914)" .
Gen Info: Giraffatitan brancai was one of the tallest sauropods, with extremely long forelimbs and neck. Its small head and peg-like teeth suggest it fed on high tree foliage, stripping leaves without chewing extensively. Its enormous body required constant feeding, likely traveling in herds across floodplains.

Name: Guanlong wucaii
Author: Xu et al.

Reference: Xu X.; Clark, J.M.; Forster, C. A.; Norell, M.A.; Erickson, G.M.; Eberth, D.A.; Jia, C. & Zhao, Q. (2006). "A basal tyrannosauroid dinosaur from the Late Jurassic of China".
Gen Info: Guanlong wucaii was a small, crested tyrannosauroid from the Late Jurassic of China. Its long, slender body, lightweight limbs, and sharp teeth indicate it was an agile predator. The head crest may have been used for display or species recognition. Likely hunted small vertebrates in forested habitats.

Name: Kentrosaurus aethiopicus
Author: Hennig

Gen Info: Kentrosaurus aethiopicus was a medium-sized stegosaur from the Late Jurassic of Africa. It had two rows of plates along its back and long tail spikes for defense. Its small head and leaf-shaped teeth indicate it fed on low vegetation. Likely moved slowly and foraged in herds to deter predators.
Habitat: Plains, lightly forested regions, open woodlands

Name: Klamelisaurus gobiensis
Author: Zhao

Gen Info: Klamelisaurus gobiensis was a long-necked sauropod from the Late Jurassic of China. Its moderately slender body and long neck allowed it to browse mid to high vegetation, including conifers and cycads. Likely lived in small herds for protection and traveled across semi-arid floodplains.

Name: Limusaurus inextricabilis

Fossil evidence suggests it was covered in feathers, making it closely related to modern birds and indicating it was an active and intelligent predator.

It had a small head with a toothless beak, long arms, and extremely long legs, making it one of the fastest dinosaurs known. Its large eyes suggest good vision, and it likely used speed to escape predators rather than fighting. Gallimimus may have fed on plants, small animals, insects, and eggs.

Name: Giganotosaurus carolinii
Author: Coria & Salgado
Material: Partial skeleton with skull, referred incomplete dentary, teeth.
Reference: Coria and Salgado, (1995). A new giant carnivorous dinosaur from the Cretaceous of Patagonia.
Gen Info: Giganotosaurus carolinii was one of the largest carnivorous dinosaurs ever discovered, even longer than Tyrannosaurus rex. It lived in South America during the Late Cretaceous period. This massive predator had a long skull with sharp, blade-like teeth designed for slicing flesh. Its powerful legs suggest it could pursue large prey, possibly hunting giant sauropods either alone or in groups.

Name: Gigantoraptor erlianensis
Author: Xu, Tan, Wang, Zhao & Tan
Material: Incomplete skeleton, mandibles.
Reference: Xu, Tan, Wang, Zhao and Tan, (2007). A gigantic bird-like dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of China.
Gen Info: Gigantoraptor erlianensis was a gigantic, feathered oviraptorosaur from Asia. Despite its intimidating size, it had a toothless beak and is believed to have been omnivorous. Its long legs indicate it could move quickly, and its feathers may have been used for display or temperature regulation. Fossils suggest it may have guarded its nests, similar to modern birds.

Name: Gilmoreosaurus mongoliensis
Author: Brett-Surman
Material: At least four individuals.
Reference: Prieto-Márquez, A. & M.A. Norell, (2010). Anatomy and Relationships of Gilmoreosaurus mongoliensis (Dinosauria: Hadrosauroidea) from the Late Cretaceous of Central Asia.
Gen Info: Gilmoreosaurus mongoliensis was a medium-sized hadrosaurid dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Asia. It had a strong beak and complex teeth that allowed it to efficiently process plant material. This dinosaur likely lived and traveled in herds, which helped protect individuals from predators.

Name: Gorgosaurus libratus
Author: Lambe
Material: Many skeletons and skulls (include almost complete skeleton with skull).
Reference:
Currie (2003) Cranial anatomy of tyrannosaurid dinosaurs from the Late Cretaceous of Alberta, Canada.
Mortimer - Theropod database (online).
Gen Info: Gorgosaurus libratus was a large tyrannosaurid predator closely related to Albertosaurus. It had a more slender and agile build compared to Tyrannosaurus rex, allowing it to move faster. With sharp teeth, strong jaws, and excellent binocular vision, Gorgosaurus was an efficient hunter that preyed on large herbivorous dinosaurs.

Name: Lambeosaurus lambei
Author: Parks
Material: At least over a dozen individuals (include skulls and skeletons).
Reference: Eberth & Evans (2014) Hadrosaurs.
Gen Info: Lambeosaurus lambei was a large hadrosaurid dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous period, well known for its hollow cranial crest shaped like a hatchet. This crest was connected to its nasal passages and was likely used to produce sounds for communication within herds, as well as for visual display. It had a long, stiff tail, a beak for cropping plants, and hundreds of teeth arranged in dental batteries for grinding tough vegetation. Lambeosaurus was a social animal that traveled in large groups and could walk both on two legs and four legs depending on its activity.

Name: Lambeosaurus magnicristatus
Author: Wilfarth
Material: At least 2 partial skeletons with skulls.
Reference: Evans, D. C., & Reisz, R. R. (2007). Anatomy and Relationships o fLambeosaurus magnicristatus, a crested hadrosaurid dinosaur (Ornithischia) from the Dinosaur Park Formation, Alberta.
Gen Info: Lambeosaurus magnicristatus was a closely related species distinguished by its much larger and more elaborate crest. This dinosaur lived in the same general regions as other lambeosaurines but may have used its unique crest shape to identify members of its own species. It was well adapted for long-distance travel and seasonal migration, feeding on a wide variety of plants. Fossil evidence suggests it lived in herds and relied on group behavior for protection against predators.

Name: Maiasaura peeblesorum
Author: Horner & Makela
Material: More than 200 individuals in all age ranges.
Reference: Albert Prieto-Marquez and Merrilee F. Guenther (2018). Perinatal specimens of Maiasaura from the Upper Cretaceous of Montana (USA): insights into the early ontogeny of saurolophine hadrosaurid dinosaurs.
Gen Info: Maiasaura peeblesorum was a medium-sized duck-billed dinosaur famous for providing the first strong evidence of parental care in dinosaurs. Fossils show nesting colonies where adults fed and protected their young until they were able to move on their own. Maiasaura had a broad beak, strong jaws, and hundreds of teeth for processing plants. It lived in large herds and likely migrated seasonally in search of food and suitable nesting grounds.

Name: Majungasaurus crenatissimus
Author: Lavocat
Material: At least more than 20 individuals.
Reference: Mortimer - Theropod database (online).
Gen Info: Majungasaurus crenatissimus was a theropod predator that lived on the island of Madagascar during the Late Cretaceous. It had a short, deep skull with thick bones and a small horn on top of its head. Its arms were very short, but its jaws were powerful and well suited for biting prey. Bite marks on fossils suggest that Majungasaurus sometimes practiced cannibalism. It lived in a warm climate with seasonal droughts.

Name: Moros intrepidus
Author: Zanno et al.
Material: Incomplete femur, incomplete tibia, fragmentary metatarsal II, incomplete metatarsal IV, phalanx IV-3 and phalanx IV-4. Referred tooth (uncertain) (teeth (uncertain)).
Reference: Zanno, L.E., Tucker, R.T., Canoville, A., Avrahami, H.M., Gates, T.A., Makovicky, P.J. (2019). "Diminutive fleet-footed tyrannosauroid narrows the 70-million-year gap in the North American fossil record".
Gen Info: Moros intrepidus was a small, early relative of the giant tyrannosaurs that appeared later. Despite its modest size, it already had advanced senses, including keen vision and hearing. Its long legs indicate it was fast and agile, making it an effective hunter of small animals. Moros represents an important evolutionary step that shows how tyrannosaurs became dominant predators over time.

Name: Morrosaurus antarcticus
Author: Rozadilla et al.
Material: Fragmentary right hind limb. Referred distal end of a (uncertain)right pedal phalanx and seven unidentified fragments (could be the same individual with holotype).
Reference: Rozadilla, S., Agnolin, F. L., Novas, F. E., Aranciaga Rolando, A. M., Motta, M. J., Lirio, J. M., & Isasi, M. P. (2016). A new ornithopod (Dinosauria, Ornithischia) from the Upper Cretaceous of Antarctica and its palaeobiogeographical implications.
Gen Info: Morrosaurus antarcticus was a small herbivorous dinosaur that lived in Antarctica when the continent was much warmer than today. It inhabited polar forests and had to survive long periods of darkness during winter months. Its body structure suggests it was a fast runner, possibly to escape predators. Morrosaurus likely lived in herds and fed on low-growing plants and shrubs.

Name: Mosaiceratops azumai
Author: Zheng, Jin & Xu
Material: Partial skull and partial skeleton.
Reference: Zheng, Jin i Xu, (2015). A psittacosaurid-like basal neoceratopsian from the Upper Cretaceous of central China and its implications for basal ceratopsian evolution.
Gen Info: Mosaiceratops azumai was a small and primitive ceratopsian dinosaur that lived during the Early Cretaceous. It had a short frill, a parrot-like beak, and relatively simple facial features compared to later horned dinosaurs. This species helps scientists understand the early evolution of ceratopsians. It was likely a social animal and fed on low vegetation in forested environments.

Name: Murusraptor barrosaensis
Author: Coria & Currie
Material: Partial skeleton with incomplete skull.
Reference: Corria & Currie (2016). A New Megaraptoran Dinosaur (Dinosauria, Theropoda, Megaraptoridae) from the Late Cretaceous of Patagonia.
Gen Info: Murusraptor barrosaensis was a large carnivorous dinosaur belonging to the megaraptorid group. It had a long skull, powerful jaws, and especially long arms equipped with sharp claws used to capture prey. Murusraptor was an active predator and one of the top hunters in its ecosystem. It lived in open environments where it could pursue large herbivorous dinosaurs.

Name: Muyelensaurus pecheni
Author: Calvo, González-Riga & Porfiri
Material: At least five individuals.
Reference: Calvo, J.O.; González-Riga, B.J.; and Porfiri, J.D. (2007) "A new titanosaur sauropod from the Late Cretaceous of Neuquén, Patagonia, Argentina.".
Gen Info: Muyelensaurus pecheni was a medium-sized sauropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of South America. It had a long neck and tail, a relatively light body for a sauropod, and pillar-like legs that supported its weight. Muyelensaurus fed on vegetation at different heights, using its long neck to reach leaves and branches. It likely lived and moved in groups, which helped protect juveniles from predators and allowed efficient use of food resources.

Name: Nodosaurus textilis
Author: Marsh
Material: Partial skeleton, referred 1 (2 (uncertain)) individuals (uncertain)
Reference: Glut, (1997). Dinosaurs - The Encyclopedia.
Gen Info: Nodosaurus textilis was a heavily armored dinosaur belonging to the nodosaurid group. Its body was covered in thick bony plates called osteoderms, providing strong protection against large predators. Unlike ankylosaurs, it did not have a tail club. Nodosaurus had a low-slung body and a small head with a beak, adapted for feeding on low-growing plants. It moved slowly but relied on its armor rather than speed for defense.

Name: Olorotitan arharensis
Author: Godefroit, Bolotsky & Alifanov
Material: Two partial skeletons and skull.
Reference: Godefroit, P., Bolotsky, Y.L. & Bolotsky, I.Y. (2012). Osteology and relationships of Olorotitan arharensis, a hollow crested hadrosaurid dinosaur from the latest Cretaceous of Far Eastern Russia.
Gen Info: Olorotitan arharensis was a large hadrosaurid dinosaur with an elegant, elongated neck and a hollow crest on its head. The crest likely played a role in sound production and visual communication within herds. Olorotitan lived in social groups and migrated through river valleys in search of food. Its posture and body shape suggest it could feed both at ground level and higher vegetation.

Name: Oohkotokia horneri
Author: Penkalski
Material: Several individuals (include skulls).
Reference: Penkalski, P. (2018). Revised systematics of the armoured dinosaur Euoplocephalus and its allies.
Gen Info: Oohkotokia horneri was a stocky, low-bodied ankylosaurid dinosaur with heavy armor covering its back and sides. It also possessed a strong tail club, which it could swing to defend itself against predators by breaking bones or delivering powerful blows. Oohkotokia fed on tough, low-growing plants and shrubs. Its body was well adapted for life close to the ground.

Name: Oviraptor philoceratops
Author: Osborn
Material: Partial skeleton with incomplete skull. Referred 15 eggs, embryo (or nestling).
Reference: Osborn, (1924). Three new Theropoda, Protoceratops zone, central Mongolia.
Gen Info: Oviraptor philoceratops was a small, lightweight theropod dinosaur with a toothless beak and a short tail. Fossil discoveries show individuals preserved sitting on nests, indicating brooding behavior similar to modern birds. It likely had feathers and was intelligent and agile. Oviraptor fed on a varied diet, possibly including eggs, small animals, and plant material.

Name: Pachyrhinosaurus canadensis
Author: Sternberg
Material: Many individuals.
Reference: Ronald S. Tykoski, Anthony R. Fiorillo & Kentaro Chiba (2019). New data and diagnosis for the Arctic ceratopsid dinosaur Pachyrhinosaurus perotorum.
Gen Info: Pachyrhinosaurus canadensis was a large ceratopsian dinosaur adapted to cold northern climates. Instead of long horns, it had a thick, bony nasal boss on its snout, which may have been used in head-to-head combat or display. It lived in massive herds that likely migrated seasonally. Its powerful beak allowed it to process tough vegetation.

Name: Pachyrhinosaurus lakustai
Author: Currie, Langston & Tanke
Material: At least 15 individuals.
Reference: Currie, P.J., Langston, W., and Tanke, D.H. (2008). "A new species of Pachyrhinosaurus (Dinosauria, Ceratopsidae) from the Upper Cretaceous of Alberta, Canada.
Gen Info: Pachyrhinosaurus lakustai was an earlier species of Pachyrhinosaurus with similar physical traits, including a thick nasal boss and a large frill. It lived in herds and shared its environment with other large herbivores and predators. This species shows how Pachyrhinosaurus evolved over time.

Name: Pentaceratops sternbergii
Author: Osborn
Material: Over a dozen individuals.
Reference: Lehman, T.M., (1998), "A gigantic skull and skeleton of the horned dinosaur Pentaceratops sternbergi from New Mexico".
Gen Info: Pentaceratops sternbergii was a large horned dinosaur with one of the longest skulls of any land animal. It had multiple facial horns and a wide frill that may have been used for display and species recognition. Pentaceratops was a powerful quadrupedal herbivore that fed on low-growing plants and shrubs.

Name: Parasaurolophus cyrtocristatus
Author: Ostrom
Material: At least 2 individuals (include partial skeleton and skull).
Reference: Sullivan, R.S.; Williamson, T.E. (1999). "A new skull of Parasaurolophus (Dinosauria: Hadrosauridae) from the Kirtland Formation of New Mexico and a revision of the genus".
Gen Info: Parasaurolophus cyrtocristatus was a large hadrosaurid dinosaur easily recognized by its long, curved hollow crest extending backward from the skull. This crest was connected to the nasal passages and could produce loud, low-frequency sounds used for communication, warning signals, and social interaction. Parasaurolophus lived in large herds and was capable of walking both on two legs and four legs. Its complex dental batteries allowed it to grind tough plant material efficiently.

Name: Parasaurolophus tubicen
Author: Wiman
Material: At least 2 individuals (skulls).
Reference: Sullivan, R.S.; Williamson, T.E. (1999). "A new skull of Parasaurolophus (Dinosauria: Hadrosauridae) from the Kirtland Formation of New Mexico and a revision of the genus".
Gen Info: Parasaurolophus tubicen was a close relative of P. cyrtocristatus but had an even longer and straighter crest. This species likely produced deeper and more powerful sounds than other hadrosaurs. It lived near river systems and wetlands, where vegetation was abundant. Parasaurolophus tubicen was highly social and depended on herd behavior for protection against predators.

Gen Info: Rhabdodon priscus was a robust ornithopod dinosaur that lived in Europe during the Late Cretaceous. It had strong jaws and thick teeth adapted for chewing tough, fibrous plants. Its body was well built, allowing it to survive in dry and seasonal environments. Rhabdodon likely lived in small groups and relied on strength rather than speed to avoid predators.

Name: Spinosaurus aegyptiacus
Author: Stromer

It had a long, narrow skull similar to that of a crocodile, conical teeth for catching fish, and a large sail on its back formed by elongated spines. Spinosaurus was specially adapted to a semi-aquatic lifestyle, spending much of its time hunting in rivers and swamps.

Name: Styracosaurus albertensis
Author: Lambe

Gen Info: Styracosaurus albertensis was a ceratopsian dinosaur distinguished by long spikes radiating from its neck frill and a prominent nasal horn. These features were likely used for display, species recognition, and defense. It lived in herds and fed on low-growing plants using its sharp beak and strong jaws.

Name: Styracosaurus ovatus
Author: Gilmore
Material: 2 (uncertain) partial skulls.
Reference: Wilson JP, Ryan MJ, Evans DC. (2020). A new, transitional centrosaurine ceratopsid from the Upper Cretaceous Two Medicine Formation of Montana and the evolution of the 'Styracosaurus-line' dinosaurs.
Gen Info: Styracosaurus ovatus was a closely related species with a slightly different arrangement of frill spikes. It shared similar behavior, living in social groups and using its horns for defense against predators. Fossil evidence suggests it occupied slightly different ecological niches.

Name: Tarbosaurus bataar
Author: Rozhdestvensky
Material: At least more than 30 individuals (include partial skeletons and skulls).

Maleev, (1955). New carnivorous dinosaurs from the Upper Cretaceous of Mongolia.

Gen Info: Tarbosaurus bataar was a massive tyrannosaurid predator from Asia and one of the apex carnivores of the Late Cretaceous. It had powerful jaws, sharp teeth, and excellent vision. Tarbosaurus hunted large herbivorous dinosaurs and dominated its ecosystem much like Tyrannosaurus rex in North America.

Name: Therizinosaurus cheloniformis

Reference: Zanno, L. E. (2010). A taxonomic and phylogenetic re-evaluation of Therizinosauria (Dinosauria: Maniraptora).
Gen Info: Therizinosaurus cheloniformis was a strange-looking theropod with an enormous body, long neck, and extremely long claws on its hands. Despite its intimidating appearance, it was mainly herbivorous, using its claws to pull branches closer. Its wide torso suggests a large digestive system for processing plant material.

These horns were used for defense against predators and possibly for dominance battles within the species. Triceratops had a powerful beak and strong jaws capable of slicing through tough vegetation, and it lived in large populations across western North America.

It lived during the very end of the Cretaceous period and shared its environment with Tyrannosaurus rex. Its body was built for strength rather than speed, and it relied on its horns and frill for protection.

T. rex had excellent vision, a strong sense of smell, and muscular legs for short bursts of speed. It was both a hunter and a scavenger, dominating its ecosystem as an apex predator.

Name: Velociraptor mongoliensis
Author: Osborn

Reference: Turner, A. H., Makovicky, P. J., & Norell, M. A. (2012). A Review of Dromaeosaurid Systematics and Paravian Phylogeny.
Gen Info: Velociraptor mongoliensis was a small but highly intelligent predatory dinosaur covered in feathers. It had a long, stiff tail for balance and a large sickle-shaped claw on each foot used to subdue prey. Velociraptor lived in harsh desert environments and relied on speed, agility, and strategy rather than strength.

Maidment, S.C.R., Brassey, C., Barrett, P.M. (2015). "The Postcranial Skeleton of an Exceptionally Complete Individual of the Plated Dinosaur Stegosaurus stenops (Dinosauria: Thyreophora) from the Upper Jurassic Morrison Formation of Wyoming.

The plates may have been used for display or temperature regulation, while the tail spikes were used for defense. Stegosaurus had a small head and fed on low-growing plants.

Its long legs suggest it was faster and more agile, and fossil evidence indicates it may have hunted in groups. Albertosaurus was a top predator in its environment and relied on speed and teamwork to bring down prey.
